the startle response in the rainbow trout is associated with Fos‐like immunoreactivity in the Mauthner cells and other neurons of the brain and the spinal cord that are known or proposed to participate in the response.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of neuronal populations in the brainstem and spinal cord that are activated during a startle‐like response.
the identification of neuronal structures involved in the startle reflex of the fish.
the identification of the neuronal circuitry involved in the startle reflex of the rainbow trout, Oncorhynchusmykiss.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Fos‐like immunoreactivity was not a specific marker for the startle response.
the Mauthner‐related neurons are not involved in the initiation of the fast escape behavior in the rainbow trout.
, although the Mauthner system plays an important role in the initiation of startle responses, it is not the only neuronal pathway that is activated during this behaviour.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the startle response involves a large number of cells, many of them not yet known to participate in this behavior, and that the startle circuitry is distributed over the brain and spinal cord.

Fos‐like staining in the startle‐evoked fish was found in the brain stem and the spinal cord in cell groups that had been proposed or known to participate in startle responses and in cell groups that until now had not been shown to participate.

Fos‐like immunoreactivity in the brainstem and spinal cord of the trout is a good marker for the activity of neurons during startle responses, and that the startle response involves a large number of neurons in the brain and spinal cord.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we found a large number of Fos‐positive neurons in the brain and the spinal cord in response to the startle response.
Fos is a useful tool for studying the neural basis of behavior.
